Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation did not change the change in BDI-II depressive symptom score compared with placebo in all subjects.
Sentence: "At the end of the study, there were no significant differences in Δ BDI-II score (score at the end of the study minus score at baseline), regardless of analysing all subjects, subjects with or without psycopharmaca, or if performing subgroup analyses based on baseline and final serum 25(OH)D levels combined with categories of baseline BDI-II scores >4 or >13."
Measured as: Δ BDI-II score (Beck Depression Inventory-II)
Population: 408 adults (mean age ~52 years) randomised to vitamin D or placebo; few clinically depressed
Intervention: Vitamin D 100,000 IU bolus followed by 20,000 IU per week for 4 months
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 408
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Elderly people with prediabetes receiving weekly vitamin D3 had lower depression scores (PHQ-9) than controls at 6 months.
Sentence: "Supplemented participants demonstrated lower mean PHQ-9 scores compared to controls at 6 (15.69 ± 6.15 vs. 19.77 ± 8.96, p = 0.021) and 12 months (13.52 ± 5.01 vs. 20.20 ± 8.67, p < 0.001)."
Measured as: PHQ-9 score at 6 months
Population: Elderly people with prediabetes (mean age ~73-74 years)
Intervention: Vitamin D3 25,000 IU weekly for 12 months, plus lifestyle measures
Comparator: No supplementation, plus lifestyle measures
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 90
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml
